name: Vilon

lead: Vilon is a two-amino-acid peptide (lysine and glutamic acid) developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group in St. Petersburg and described as an immune-system and anti-aging "bioregulator". People discuss it in longevity circles, with a looks payoff that is the hope of slower tissue ageing and a younger appearance.

Khavinson's group proposes that Vilon loosens condensed chromatin in ageing lymphocytes and so reactivates silenced genes, reported from cell cultures. Published work is mostly cell-culture and mouse experiments, including effects on tumour development and lifespan in mice, much of it from the originating institute. No controlled human trial of Vilon was found and no appearance effect is established.

paras: It is sold as a research peptide and discussed in short-course bioregulator routines in longevity communities. Any visible effect on appearance is a hope rather than a documented result.
No systematic human safety data were found. It is not an approved drug in the US or EU and is sold as a research peptide.

angle.text: Vilon is a Lys-Glu peptide from Khavinson's bioregulator program, discussed as an anti-aging candidate on the idea that it slows tissue ageing and so a younger look. Data come from cell and mouse studies; no human trials are known.

lead: Vilon is a synthetic dipeptide made of the amino acids lysine and glutamic acid (Lys-Glu). It was developed by the Russian gerontologist Vladimir Khavinson and colleagues at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology as part of a program on short peptide "bioregulators". [1] People interested in anti-ageing peptides take it as a longevity and immune-support compound, with the hope of slowing the age-related changes that show up in how a person looks and ages over time.

The originating group describes Vilon as an immunomodulatory, thymus-like peptide that acts epigenetically: in cultured lymphocytes from elderly donors it is reported to loosen condensed chromatin and reactivate silenced genes. [1][2] Published work includes cell-culture and mouse experiments, such as a 2002 study comparing Vilon and Epitalon in tumour-prone transgenic mice, [3] and a set of Russian clinical studies in older patients, including patients with diabetes and with colorectal cancer. [4][5][6]

Most of the literature comes from the originating institute and is published largely in Russian journals. Vilon is not an approved medicine in the US or EU and is sold as a research peptide. No study has measured its effect on skin, hair or facial appearance.

paras: Vilon is a two-residue peptide, L-lysyl-L-glutamic acid, with a molecular weight of about 275 g/mol. [1] It belongs to a family of short peptides (di-, tri- and tetrapeptides) that Khavinson's group describes as bioregulators acting on gene expression; related entries include Epitalon. [1] Other short peptides from the same research tradition, such as the tripeptide KED (Lys-Glu-Asp), have been reviewed for neuroprotective effects in Alzheimer's disease models. [7][8]

According to an AI-generated encyclopedia summary, Khavinson's group moved in the 1980s and 1990s from extracting polypeptide complexes from animal organs, such as Thymalin, to synthesising short peptides, and Vilon was introduced as a synthetic immunomodulatory dipeptide in the late 1990s. [1] An early report in 2000 described subcutaneous Vilon inhibiting spontaneous tumour growth and increasing mean lifespan in mice. [1] Russian clinical reports followed in the mid-2000s. [4][5][6]

The originating group proposes an epigenetic mechanism. A 2006 article on anti-ageing peptide bioregulators reports that such peptides induce reactivation of chromatin, [2] and a summary of the group's work describes Vilon as decondensing facultative heterochromatin and activating ribosomal gene regions in cultured lymphocytes from elderly donors, with effects described as stronger in older cells. [1] These findings come largely from one research network, and no independent human replication was found.

A randomised study of Vilon, described as a thymomimetic, examined its effect on the blood coagulation and fibrinolysis systems in patients with type 1 diabetes of different ages. [4] A related clinical trial looked at its effect on immune status and coagulation haemostasis in diabetes patients of different ages. [5] A controlled clinical trial described the group's initial experience adding Vilon to the treatment of elderly patients with stage III colon and rectal cancer; the authors concluded that preliminary results supported its use to improve two-year survival and reduce post-operative complications and recurrences. [6] These reports were published in Advances in Gerontology, a Russian journal, and are not independent confirmations.

Several small Russian clinical studies have been published: in type 1 diabetes patients (coagulation and fibrinolysis), in diabetes patients (immune status and coagulation), and in elderly colorectal cancer patients receiving it alongside standard treatment. [4][5][6] No study has tested Vilon for skin, hair or visible ageing. In transgenic mice prone to mammary tumours, monthly injections of Vilon did not change tumour induction through 9 months, while Epitalon was associated with inhibited carcinogenesis later in life. [3]
No systematic safety data from independent human trials were found. Vilon is not approved as a drug in the US or EU and is available through research-peptide sellers.
